Hi everyone,

I’m looking for a good inventory sync app for Shopify. We have a lot of products and updating inventory manually across stores is becoming difficult.

I’ve looked at a few apps on the Shopify App Store, but I’m not sure which ones are actually reliable.

You’re going to get a lot of suggestions. You might want to clarify exactly what you’re looking for in an inventory app. Yes, you have multiple locations… but are you looking at Receiving (POs), Stock Takes, Transfers, etc.

I can say our app will help you with all of that though - check out FyreTrail and see if that’s the right app for you. You can find more on our web site (fyretrail.com) as well to see what it’s all about and see if that aligns with what you’re looking to solve.

Reliability is definitely a question to ask and is going to be a tough one to really get a handle on considering the current landscape with Stocky sunsetting. There’s been a large amount of apps that have hit the market in the last month or so. It’s a bit daunting at how many there are. I would go for something that’s been around longer than that. For reference, we’ve been “alive” for almost two years now and have been on the Shopify App Store since Jan. 30th. We’ve had a large amount of stores install and have a solid customer base using the app constantly from all over the world. Hopefully that adds a bit of credibility for FyreTrail.

Good Luck!

posts.cooked:
Hey @woysanstore ,

If you’re syncing inventory between multiple Shopify stores, I’d look at more than just the app rating. Things like real-time syncing, SKU matching, multi location support, error logs, and how responsive the support team is can make a big difference.

I’ve seen Multi Store Sync Power mentioned quite a bit for this type of setup. It supports real time inventory syncing between stores, two way sync, and multi location inventory. It also has error reports and detailed logs, which I think are pretty important when you have a large catalog.

I’d definitely test any app with a small group of products first before syncing the whole catalog. Inventory mistakes can get messy pretty quickly if the SKUs or product mapping aren’t set up correctly.

Thank You!
This post was flagged by the community and is temporarily hidden.

One question I’d add is: what happens when inventory is moving, not just syncing?

Most evaluations focus on whether stock updates appear in another store quickly, but operational issues often show up around the workflows that change inventory in the first place:

  • Receiving inventory
  • Transfers between locations
  • Adjustments
  • Cycle counts
  • Returns

We’ve found that “inventory sync” and “inventory accuracy” aren’t always the same thing. A system can synchronize counts perfectly and still create reconciliation work if teams can’t easily trace why inventory changed.

When testing solutions, I’d look not only at synchronization speed, but also whether every inventory change has a clear audit trail showing:

  • Who made the change
  • What document triggered it
  • Which location was affected
  • What the inventory position was before and after

That visibility tends to become more important as operations grow across multiple stores and locations.

One option worth checking out is Inventory Sync – GoGo. It’s designed specifically for syncing inventory across multiple Shopify stores, so it could be a good fit if you have a large catalog and want to avoid manual updates.

It can automatically sync inventory across connected stores in real time, which makes it much easier to keep stock levels consistent across stores.

posts.cooked:
Hi @woysanstore

It really depends on your workflow, but reliability and sync speed would be the two things I’d focus on most.

We’ve learned that the biggest problem isn’t usually syncing inventory itself—it’s what happens when inventory doesn’t sync quickly enough. That’s when oversells, manual corrections, and customer service issues start appearing.

If you’re managing multiple Shopify stores, I’d look for an app that supports real-time inventory updates, inventory sharing between stores, and clear sync logs so you can easily track what happened if something goes wrong.

We’ve had a good experience with Easify Inventory Sync for syncing inventory across Shopify stores. One thing I like is that it supports shared inventory pools, so multiple products or stores can draw from the same stock source without having to manually adjust quantities everywhere.

That said, before choosing any app, I’d recommend thinking about your specific use case:

  • Multiple Shopify stores selling the same products?

  • Shared inventory between different products or variants?

  • Multi-location inventory?

  • Bundles that need to deduct component stock?

Different inventory sync apps tend to be stronger in different areas.

If you can share a bit more about your setup (multiple stores, locations, bundles, etc.), people here can probably give more targeted recommendations.

@woysanstore “sync” usually means one of three jobs.

  1. Multiple Shopify locations: native inventory per location plus transfers. No extra app required for that.
  2. Shopify plus Amazon/eBay/other storefronts: that is a channel sync app. If oversells are the issue, look for event-driven updates, not a 15 minute poll.
  3. A warehouse floor that has to match Shopify: bins, receive, pick. That is a WMS, not a sync tool.

SKUSavvy is #3, not #2. I work on it (mobile WMS, 3D map, pick routing, two-way Shopify sync).

ai_summary.summarized_text:
The original request is for a reliable way to keep inventory updated across Shopify stores with a large catalog, but the exact setup—separate storefronts, multiple locations, marketplaces, or an external inventory source—remains unspecified. Replies stress that these are different problems and that the right tool depends on where stock is managed and which system is the source of truth.

Suggested options include FyreTrail for receiving, transfers, adjustments, and multi-location workflows; several store-sync apps, including Multi Store Sync Power, GoGo, Easify, and EagleLytics; and broader channel or warehouse tools such as Nventory and SKUSavvy. Many recommendations come from app vendors, so they are not independent evaluations. A recurring concern is scheduled syncing, which can leave oversell windows; participants recommend checking whether updates are event-driven, along with SKU matching, location support, error alerts, audit logs, and handling of simultaneous changes, refunds, and cancellations.

No app was selected, and key questions about the number of stores, inventory ownership, channels, catalog size, and order volume remain unanswered. Replies recommend testing a small, representative set of SKUs before a full rollout; one also suggests consolidating brands into a single Shopify store if separate checkouts and inventory are unnecessary.
